prompt: In the section's comparison of acetone with ethane, what pK_a is given for acetone?
explanation: Acetone has pK_a = 19.3, while ethane has pK_a ≈ 60. Table 22.5.1 rounds the value for a ketone to 19.

prompt: Comparing acetone (pK_a = 19.3) with ethane (pK_a ≈ 60), the neighboring carbonyl group increases acidity by a factor of 10 to about what power?
explanation: The section says the carbonyl group increases the acidity of the ketone over the alkane by a factor of 10^40. (60 − 19.3 ≈ 40.7 pK_a units, which the section rounds to 40.)

prompt: Over which atoms is the negative charge of an enolate ion shared?

choices.text: The oxygen and the α carbon
Only the α carbon
choices.why: Resonance spreads the charge onto the electronegative oxygen, which is what stabilizes the enolate ion.

choices.text: Only the carbonyl carbon
choices.why: The charge is shared by the oxygen and the α carbon, not the carbonyl carbon.

choices.text: The α carbon and the β carbon
choices.why: The charge is shared with the oxygen through overlap with the carbonyl p orbitals. The β carbon isn't part of that π system.

explanation: The enolate ion is stabilized by resonance: the negative charge is shared by the electronegative oxygen and the α carbon, as the electrostatic potential map in Figure 22.5.1 shows.

prompt: Which statement describes the α carbon of an enolate ion?

choices.text: It is sp2-hybridized, and its p orbital overlaps the carbonyl p orbitals
It is sp3-hybridized, and the negative charge stays on it
choices.why: In the enolate the α carbon is sp2, so its p orbital can overlap the carbonyl p orbitals and share the charge with oxygen.

choices.text: It is sp-hybridized, like a carbon in a triple bond
choices.why: The α carbon has three σ bonds plus a p orbital, so it is sp2.

choices.text: It is sp2-hybridized, but its p orbital is perpendicular to the carbonyl p orbitals
choices.why: If the orbitals didn't overlap, the oxygen couldn't share the charge and there would be no resonance stabilization.

explanation: The α carbon of the enolate ion is sp2-hybridized and has a p orbital that overlaps the neighboring carbonyl p orbitals. So the negative charge is shared by the electronegative oxygen, and the enolate ion is resonance-stabilized.

prompt: How must the α C–H bond be oriented for a base to abstract the proton?

choices.text: Roughly parallel to the p orbitals of the carbonyl group
Perpendicular to the p orbitals of the carbonyl group
choices.why: The section says proton abstraction occurs when the C–H bond is roughly parallel to the carbonyl p orbitals.

choices.text: Pointing directly at the carbonyl oxygen
choices.why: What matters is alignment with the carbonyl p orbitals, so the new p orbital on the α carbon can overlap them.

choices.text: Orientation doesn't matter for proton abstraction
choices.why: The section states that abstraction occurs when the bond is oriented roughly parallel to the carbonyl p orbitals.

explanation: Proton abstraction from a carbonyl compound occurs when the α C–H bond is oriented roughly parallel to the p orbitals of the carbonyl group, so the resulting p orbital on the α carbon overlaps the carbonyl π system (Figure 22.5.1).

prompt: Why does sodium ethoxide deprotonate acetone only to the extent of about 0.1%?

choices.text: Acetone (pK_a 19.3) is a weaker acid than ethanol (pK_a 16)
Acetone is a stronger acid than ethanol
choices.why: It's the other way round: ethanol (pK_a 16) is the stronger acid, so the equilibrium favors acetone and ethoxide.

choices.text: Acetone's α hydrogens aren't acidic at all
choices.why: They are weakly acidic. A more powerful base such as LDA removes them completely.

choices.text: Ethoxide is too sterically hindered to reach the α hydrogens
choices.why: The section's reason is the relative acid strengths: ethanol is a stronger acid than acetone.

explanation: Because carbonyl compounds are only weakly acidic, a strong base is needed. With an alkoxide such as sodium ethoxide, deprotonation of acetone takes place only to about 0.1% because acetone is a weaker acid than ethanol (pK_a = 16). A more powerful base converts the carbonyl compound completely into its enolate ion.

prompt: To about what extent, in percent, does sodium ethoxide deprotonate acetone?
explanation: Deprotonation takes place only to the extent of about 0.1%, because acetone (pK_a 19.3) is a weaker acid than ethanol (pK_a 16).

prompt: Which base readily converts most carbonyl compounds completely into their enolate ions?

choices.text: Lithium diisopropylamide, LDA
Sodium ethoxide, NaOCH2CH3
choices.why: Ethoxide deprotonates acetone only to about 0.1%, because ethanol is a stronger acid than acetone.

choices.text: Diisopropylamine, HN(i-C3H7)2
choices.why: Diisopropylamine is the weak acid (pK_a 36) that LDA is made from; LDA is its lithium salt.

choices.text: Sodium methoxide, NaOCH3
choices.why: Like ethoxide, methoxide is an alkoxide. Its conjugate acid, CH3OH (pK_a 16), is more acidic than a ketone, so deprotonation is incomplete.

explanation: LDA, LiN(i-C3H7)2, is the lithium salt of the weak acid diisopropylamine (pK_a = 36), so it is a strong enough base to deprotonate most carbonyl compounds completely.

prompt: What is the pK_a of diisopropylamine, the acid from which LDA is made?
explanation: Diisopropylamine has pK_a = 36 (Table 22.5.1, dialkylamine). Because it is such a weak acid, its lithium salt, LDA, is a strong base that can readily deprotonate most carbonyl compounds.

prompt: How is LDA prepared?

choices.text: By reaction of butyllithium with diisopropylamine
By reaction of sodium ethoxide with diisopropylamine
choices.why: Ethoxide is far too weak a base to remove a proton from diisopropylamine (pK_a 36), and it would give a sodium salt, not a lithium one.

choices.text: By reaction of butyllithium with butane
choices.why: Butane is the by-product of making LDA, not a starting material.

choices.text: By reaction of a lithium enolate with diisopropylamine
choices.why: That is the reverse of enolate formation. Diisopropylamine (pK_a 36) is a much weaker acid than a ketone, so the reaction runs the other way.

explanation: LDA is easily prepared by reaction of butyllithium with diisopropylamine in tetrahydrofuran, which gives LDA and butane.

prompt: Why is LDA soluble in organic solvents?

choices.text: Because of its two alkyl (isopropyl) groups
Because it is a neutral amine, not a salt
choices.why: LDA is the lithium salt of diisopropylamine.

choices.text: Because it is a weak base
choices.why: LDA is a strong base; its conjugate acid has pK_a 36. Its solubility comes from its alkyl groups.

choices.text: Because it contains no metal
choices.why: LDA contains lithium: its formula is LiN(i-C3H7)2.

explanation: LDA, LiN(i-C3H7)2, is soluble in organic solvents because of its two alkyl groups.

prompt: According to Table 22.5.1, which compound has the most acidic C–H hydrogens?

choices.text: 2,4-Pentanedione, CH3COCH2COCH3
Acetone, CH3COCH3
choices.why: A ketone has pK_a about 19, much less acidic than a 1,3-diketone (pK_a 9).

choices.text: Methyl acetate, CH3CO2CH3
choices.why: An ester has pK_a about 25.

choices.text: N,N-Dimethylacetamide, CH3CON(CH3)2
choices.why: An N,N-dialkylamide has pK_a about 30, the least acidic of these four.

explanation: Table 22.5.1 gives pK_a values of about 9 for a 1,3-diketone, 19 for a ketone, 25 for an ester, and 30 for an N,N-dialkylamide. The lower the pK_a, the stronger the acid, so 2,4-pentanedione is the most acidic.

prompt: Using the values in Table 22.5.1, by how many pK_a units is a 1,3-diketone such as 2,4-pentanedione more acidic than a ketone such as acetone?
explanation: Table 22.5.1 lists a ketone at pK_a 19 and a 1,3-diketone at pK_a 9: 19 − 9 = 10 pK_a units. A hydrogen flanked by two carbonyl groups is much more acidic.

prompt: According to Table 22.5.1, what is the approximate pK_a of a 3-keto ester such as methyl acetoacetate, CH3COCH2CO2CH3?
explanation: Table 22.5.1 lists 3-keto esters (β-keto esters) at pK_a 11, between 1,3-diketones (9) and 1,3-diesters (13).

prompt: Why are β-dicarbonyl compounds such as 2,4-pentanedione much more acidic than simple ketones?

choices.text: Their enolate ions share the negative charge with both carbonyl oxygens
They have more α hydrogens than simple ketones
choices.why: Acidity depends on how well the anion is stabilized, not on how many α hydrogens a compound has. The most acidic hydrogens are the two on the carbon between the carbonyls.

choices.text: Their enolate ions keep the negative charge on the α carbon only
choices.why: The charge is spread over the α carbon and both carbonyl oxygens, which is the source of the extra stability.

choices.text: They are carboxylic acids, with acidic –OH hydrogens
choices.why: 2,4-Pentanedione has no –OH group. Its acidic hydrogens are on the carbon between the two carbonyls.

explanation: When a hydrogen is flanked by two carbonyl groups, its acidity is enhanced further. The enolate ions of β-dicarbonyl compounds are stabilized by sharing the negative charge with the two neighboring carbonyl oxygens; the enolate of 2,4-pentanedione has three resonance forms.

prompt: How many resonance forms does the enolate ion of 2,4-pentanedione have?
explanation: The enolate ion of 2,4-pentanedione has three resonance forms: one with the charge on the central carbon and one with the charge on each of the two carbonyl oxygens.

prompt: Rank these compounds from most acidic to least acidic: (a) 1-phenyl-1,3-butanedione, C6H5COCH2COCH3; (b) methyl 2-methylpropanoate, (CH3)2CHCO2CH3; (c) cyclopentanecarbaldehyde, a cyclopentane ring bearing a –CHO group.

choices.why: An aldehyde's α hydrogen is more acidic than an ester's, so (c) comes before (b).
A β-dicarbonyl compound such as (a) is the most acidic of the three.
This is the reverse. A carboxylic acid derivative such as the ester (b) is the least acidic.

explanation: As Worked Example 22.5.1 explains, a β-dicarbonyl compound is most acidic, a ketone or aldehyde is next, and a carboxylic acid derivative is least acidic. So the order is (a) > (c) > (b).

prompt: Which hydrogens of 1-phenyl-1,3-butanedione, C6H5COCH2COCH3, are the most acidic?

choices.text: The CH2 hydrogens between the two carbonyl groups
The CH3 hydrogens, next to one carbonyl group
choices.why: They are α to one carbonyl group and somewhat acidic, but less so than the hydrogens flanked by two carbonyls.

choices.text: The five hydrogens on the benzene ring
choices.why: Ring hydrogens are not on a carbon next to a carbonyl group, so they aren't acidic.

choices.text: The CH3 and CH2 hydrogens, all equally acidic
choices.why: The CH2 hydrogens are flanked by two carbonyl groups, which makes them more acidic than the CH3 hydrogens.

explanation: In Worked Example 22.5.1, the hydrogens on carbon 2, flanked by both carbonyl groups, are the most acidic; those on carbon 4 (the CH3) are less acidic.

prompt: How many acidic α hydrogens does methyl 2-methylpropanoate, (CH3)2CHCO2CH3, have?
explanation: The α carbon is the CH next to the carbonyl group, and it has just 1 hydrogen (Worked Example 22.5.1). The two CH3 groups on it are β, and the OCH3 hydrogens are on the far side of the ester oxygen.

prompt: How is the anion formed by removing an α hydrogen from acetonitrile, CH3C≡N, stabilized?

choices.text: By resonance that places the negative charge on nitrogen as well as on carbon
By resonance that places the negative charge on the nitrile carbon
choices.why: The resonance form that stabilizes the anion puts the charge on the electronegative nitrogen.

choices.text: It isn't stabilized, because nitriles aren't acidic
choices.why: Nitriles are acidic (pK_a about 25 in Table 22.5.1) and form enolate-like anions.

choices.text: By hydrogen bonding between the anion's carbon and nitrogen
choices.why: The stabilization comes from resonance delocalization of the charge onto nitrogen, not from hydrogen bonding.

explanation: Nitriles, too, are acidic and can be converted into enolate-like anions. The acetonitrile anion has two resonance forms, one with the negative charge on the CH2 carbon and one with it on nitrogen (Exercise 22.5.2).
